questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Hong Kong due to a combination of factors. First of all because of an interest in visiting a region affected by the crossing of cultures, and because of a wish to explore a very politically exciting area. In addition to this most people are either fluent or very good English speakers, so communication and getting around in the city is straightforward. The Chinese University of Hong Kong has a very good and broad choice of anthropology courses - my main major - which spoke a lot to me as well.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: CUHK is an excellent university: with a good study environment, many social activities to attend, and a broad choice of courses. My experience was that the level of study was a bit lower than in Denmark, but as far as I hear from students on exchange in other countries, this is very common. The courses are still both interesting and they definitely broadened my anthropological knowledge.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of information regarding covid-19, which was a bit difficult to navigate. The information regarding registration at the University and related things were much easier. Their website is somewhat packed with information though, so it takes some time to get into all the details. I recommend pairing up with other students going to CUHK from Denmark if you can.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: A lot. They a very good at making sure we have all the information we need. They communicate mostly through email, but at their office, they were always available for us if we had questions. They inform us a lot about the selection of courses. It is possible to rechoose courses upon arrival, and even to try out some courses during the first couple of weeks, to see if it is the right fit for you. Also, they arrange tours in the city, and a lot of information on the different options of activities on campus, what kinds of apps to have, have to get around in the metro, and so on.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Students were staying in different dorms. Most often (if not in every case) on a floor with multiple rooms, shared kitchen,s and bathrooms. You can choose between single, double or triple rooms. The fewer people the more expensive (but campus housing in general is very cheap! And especially when compared to the rest of Hong Kong).

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Some dorms offer the option of meals paid in advance, but my impression is that most people (including myself) just pay for/make their food during the stay. A lot of times we would go out to eat or eat at the dorm-canteens. They are mostly both nice and cheap. Most houses have kitchens, but you have to buy kitchen supplies yourself.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: During the winter months (December-February) it can get very cold in the dorms since they are not very well isolated. Bring warm closeth for these months! Also to sleep in. And go for the winters-sheet/blanket in Ikea instead of the summer one. Earplugs can also be nice if you are a light sleeper, and maybe buy a top-madras for the beds if you don't like hard ones (because they are!!).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is good help, but you need to start at a good time. Some of the stuff you need to send by mail, and it takes some time and is a bit expensive (we were two people sending together to make it cheaper).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There are a lot of documents you need to fill out and send. This takes some time, and especially in this part of the process I recommend partnering up with other students from your own university/country going to the same place - it helps a lot to have to heads to not forget anything important. It's an ongoing process from around 6-8 months before you go, so be patient and ready to put time into the things before the deadlines.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can always contact the international office at CUHK, both by phone and mail (be aware of the time difference though).

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. Also, I put a lot of time into applying for the ones I wanted before I went to Hong Kong, only to realize that I was able to choose again when a arrived. So no stress about applying for the right/perfect classes before you go. (except if you want to take a mandarin or Cantonese course - then you need to apply in advance. They send you information on this option by email.).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start in good time, don't hesitate to ask the university for help, and don't stress about choosing the right courses before you go. Also be aware that Mandarin and Cantonese classes take a lot of time and effort - which is fine if you enjoy language learning, but can also be a bit frustrating from time to time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is a bit lower than what I have experienced at the University of Copenhagen, and the expectations from the teachers are as well. But they are still very interesting and on the plus side it gives you a lot of surpluses to enjoy and dive into the lectures and topics.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching was similar in the way that the courses were mainly built up around a lecture and then a smaller seminar to discuss the readings. A big difference is that all your attendance and work count as a part of your final grade, meaning that you have less freedom to study as it best suits you.
Also I was used to having large but few courses, and at CUHK you have to have 5 courses when you are from UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Written and spoken putonghua (mandarin) (CLCP1113 and 1123)
Anthropology of Body, Love, and Emotion (anthropology)
Meanings of Life (anthropology)
Understanding Masculinities and Social Change (gender studies)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Anthropology of Body, Love, and Emotion together with Understanding Masculinities. The teachers are very good, sharp, and strong in their fields. They definitely have the heart in them, and they also demand something back from you, want to challenge you, and are open to being in dialogue. These are definitely the courses I learned the most from, and from which I attained knowledge that I use in my other studies afterward.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Only that I quickly spend a lot on food if I didn't buy kitchen supplies to cook myself.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transportation was extremely cheap. Drinks and alcohol on bars a very expensive! Drink before entering or go out on ladies' night if you are a woman.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything from dancing, tennis, swimming, fitness, kayaking, and martial arts. The university also arranges a lot of cultural activities for students to learn more about the culture of Hong Kong (food, language, art...).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Using the pool - it's very cheap and nice in the warm months. But hiking is a must-do in general! So many beautiful routes and a good way for socializing or just take a break alone and away from a life with a new and intense social and study life. 

Keep an eye on your email - they send out a lot of interesting offers.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking. Going to a meditation day at the big buddha in the plum-village temple (look it up online - it's mainly on Sundays). Take the boats from central to Peng Chau, Cheng Chau, and Lamma Islands! Especially during the warmer months. There is a good chill hippie vibe, and it's good if you need a break from the big city. Explore the city by walking around, or taking the tram to Hong Kong Island. Visit random cafés - especially Alley Coffee! They have the best light-roasted coffee. Go to a horse race at Happy Valley.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was easy, mainly because most people speak good English. As long as you are open, friendly, and respect the culture people are extremely helpful, nice, and interested in speaking with you. But there also exists a certain shyness, so don't hesitate to contact and show interest in the culture and people yourself.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be open, show interest, and ask questions yourself! Then most people are very interested in getting to know you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: My experience was that people don't tell you directly if they feel like you have done something wrong or stepped over a line. This can be good to pay attention to since it is easier to accidentally cross some lines when you are two people from very different cultures staying together.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness, politeness, and how helpful people were.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Bring warm closeth for when the unexpected cold comes. 
Bring some nice stuff for your room to make it homely.
Be open and make contact with local people yourself.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I was surprised by the richness of nature! I didn't expect that from Hong Kong, but really it is basically a big city with so much to experience, and it is both easy and fast to get around.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The fact of making a home in Hong Kong and getting to know the city as well as I did. To get local bars to go to, coffee places, and streets you know well. Just exploring all the different corners of the area. It's an amazing concrete jungle surrounded by mountains and with so much to offer.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Fomo in the beginning. To just remember to let myself take social breaks - and also study breaks. Give yourself time to adapt and do what you need to do - not always what you feel you should.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
